Q: Parser generator for Java with the following requirements A:

Take a look at SableCC. Sablecc is an easy to use parser generator that accepts the grammar of your language as EBNF, without intermingling action code, and generates a Java parser that produces a syntax tree which can be traversed using a tree node visitor. SableCC is powerful, yet much simpler to use than ANTLR, JavaCC, yacc, etc. It also does not require a separate lexer. Constructing your language processor amounts to extending a visitor class generated from your grammar, and to overriding its methods which are called upon when a syntactic construct is encountered by the parser. For every grammar rule XYZ, the visitor will have a method inAXYZ(Node xyz)....outAXYZ(Node xyz) called upon when the parser matches the rule.

Q: How do C++ object lifetime interact with arrays from C code? A:

You don’t give much detail for how this works, but it sounds to me like you’re obtaining shared memory in two different processes, from a function like shmat() or mmap(), writing the memory in one, and reading it from the other.

First, to address some widespread misconceptions: C and C++ compilers are allowed to assume that an object can only be referred to by certain types of pointers (its own type, a base type, void, signed or unsigned char or std::byte). C++23 added std::start_lifetime_as and std::start_lifetime_as_array as ways to get around that: it can for example reinterpret a uint54_t as a double if they have the same size and required alignment.

The wording of the Standard technically allows an implementation to have operations “implicitly creating objects within a region of storage,” which automatically “starts the lifetime of [...] implicit-lifetime types in its specified region of storage.” (§6.7.2(10)) but that need an additional step “producing a pointer to a suitable created object.” (§6.7.2(11)) ¹ There is some controversy over whether the wording of §7.6.1.9(14), “if the original pointer value points to an object a, and there is an object b of type similar to T that is pointer-interconvertible with a, the result is a pointer to b,” is close enough that static_cast<T*>(static_cast<void*>(p)) and reinterpret_cast<T*>(p) from initialized storage “[produce] a pointer to a suitable created object.” Some language-lawyers don’t think this counts. Some of these people believe that std::start_lifetime_as, which “creates and returns a pointer to an object a of type T,” does count, for no reason that I can see.

You never need to call std::launder on a pointer to storage. That’s just superstition. Under the interpretation of the rules that supposedly justify using it, where you need to “create objects” in certain specific ways, std::launder never says anything about creating objects, starting lifetimes or suitable created objects. In fact, it requires the caller to already have a valid pointer to an object. So it would not even guarantee the thing you supposedly need it for. (qv. §17.6.5)²

In C++23: If the payload is an implicit-lifetime type, including an array of int, calling std::start_lifetime_as or std::start_lifetime_as_array from the receiving process will implicitly create an object or objects of that type in the storage and return a pointer to the first. Per (§20.2.6), std::start_lifetime_as T>(p) creates and returns a pointer to “an object a of type T whose address is p, and objects nested within a, as follows: The object representation of a is the contents of the storage prior to the call to start_lifetime_as....” Any realistic implementation of this is going to be a pointer cast that compiles to a no-op, or at most twiddles some bits of the pointer value. The useful thing it does is allow an exception to the strict-aliasing rules. But a pointer to void, signed/unsigned char or std::byte is allowed to be freely aliased anyway (qv the C Standard). The post you link to appears to be speculating based on some early draft that the implementation would make some kind of copy, but the Standard is specifically written to allow it not to.

There doesn’t technically seem to be a way in C++23 to create a non-implicit-lifetime class in shared memory, unless you interpret [obj.lifetime] as technically saying that std::start_lifetime_as_array can start the lifetime of any complete object. In practical terms, a non-implicit-lifetime class would manage resources in the process that instantiated it. It doesn’t make sense to pass something like a fstream in shared memory and try to use file descriptors or heap allocations from some other process. You can check for this at compile-time if you want by testing std::is_implicit_lifetime_v (§21.3.5.4).

In C, C++14 or C++17, you just need to follow the strict-aliasing rules. If your shared-memory system call returns something like void*, and you create something like an unsigned char* to alias it and add offsets, you’re fine. If you cast either of those pointers to a different object pointer type, they are allowed to alias the same memory. In C++14, [object.life] says you don’t need to do anything more than obtain storage for the object and initialize it to begin its lifetime. You could convert the address in shared memory to an object pointer with static_cast (possibly after a cast to void*) or a C-style cast.

¹ No real-world compiler does, but it’s not totally ludicrous that someone, someday, will want a secure implementation where the compiler must tell the computer at runtime that a region of memory is expected to hold objects of a certain type. IBM has created hardware that requires a flag to be set on a chunk of memory for it to hold a pointer. You can therefore think of this as an extremely paranoid form of defensive coding for forward-compatibility.

² Some posters have been very active about spreading this myth. So if you see someone talking about a “new object model” or “pointer provenance” in relation to std::launder, you can be sure their confusion traces back to the same source. There is no basis for any of it in the Standard, whatsoever. The actual use of std::launder is for a few corner cases where an object is destroyed and replaced, but the compiler would otherwise be entitled to assume that a reference is still to the original object. These include a pointer to a const, complete object; or a reference to a base class that is replaced by a derived type.

Q: Java parser-generator for these requirements A:

As @Ira said, a generated parser will at least depend on a runtime that makes generic parsing options easy to invoke. The alternative would be to copy the exact same runtime code into each generated parser.

That said, I think JavaCC has the least runtime requirements: a CharStream class that you can copy from it's library.

Unfortunately, readability of generated parsers is inversely proportional to the features of the runtime. The less runtime, the lower the level, and less readability.

Given the limited scope of the Java parsing you require, you might want to analyze if what you need is achievable with just a regexp library.
